title: Jupiter
summary: The largest planet in the Solar System, a gas giant more than twice as massive as all the other planets combined.

facts.label: Surface
facts.value: None — it has no solid ground

facts.label: Great Red Spot

age6_8.summary: The biggest planet. It has a giant storm with red swirls.
age6_8.body:
Jupiter is the biggest planet in our Solar System [1].

It is so big that all the other planets could fit inside it with room to spare [1].

Jupiter is not made of rock like Earth. It is mostly gas. If you tried to land on it, there would be nothing to stand on [1].

There is a huge red storm on Jupiter called the Great Red Spot. It is wider than the whole Earth [2].

Jupiter has lots of moons — more than ninety that we know about [2].

age9_12.summary: The Solar System's largest planet, its famous storm, and its family of moons.
age9_12.body:
Jupiter is the fifth planet from the Sun and by far the largest [1].

## An enormous planet

Jupiter is about 139,800 kilometres across and has 318 times Earth's mass. It is more than twice as massive as all the other planets put together [1].

Despite its size it spins faster than any other planet, turning once in under ten hours. That fast spin squashes it slightly, so it is a little wider across the middle than from pole to pole [1].

## No ground to land on

Jupiter is a gas giant, made mostly of hydrogen and helium. Going down through it, the gas simply gets denser and hotter until it behaves like a liquid. There is no surface to stand on [1].

## The Great Red Spot

The Great Red Spot is a storm larger than Earth. Astronomers have been watching a storm in that position for more than 150 years, and possibly much longer. It has been shrinking in recent decades [2].

## Moons

Jupiter has at least 95 confirmed moons, and the count keeps rising as smaller ones are found [2].

The four largest — Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto — were spotted by Galileo in 1610. Seeing objects orbiting something other than Earth was powerful evidence that not everything went around us [2].

Europa is especially interesting: beneath its icy shell there is very likely a salty ocean, which makes it one of the best places to look for life beyond Earth [2].

teen.summary: The Solar System's most massive planet: a hydrogen-helium gas giant with a powerful magnetosphere and a large satellite system.
teen.body:
Jupiter is the fifth planet from the Sun and the most massive, at approximately 318 Earth masses — more than double the combined mass of every other planet [1].

## Structure

Jupiter is composed principally of hydrogen and helium in roughly solar proportions. It has no surface in any useful sense: with depth, gas transitions smoothly to supercritical fluid, and at extreme pressure hydrogen becomes metallic and electrically conducting [1].

Whether Jupiter has a compact rocky core or a diffuse, partially dissolved one is genuinely uncertain. Gravity measurements from the Juno mission favour a fuzzy core extending over a substantial fraction of the interior, which was not the expectation beforehand [2].

## Rotation and magnetism

Jupiter completes a rotation in under 10 hours, the fastest of any planet, producing noticeable equatorial bulging. Circulation in metallic hydrogen generates a magnetic field roughly 20,000 times stronger than Earth's, driving the largest magnetosphere of any planet and intense radiation belts [2].

## Atmosphere

Banded cloud structure arises from alternating zonal jets. The Great Red Spot is an anticyclonic storm exceeding Earth's diameter; continuous observations date from the nineteenth century, and whether earlier seventeenth-century reports describe the same feature is not settled. It has measurably contracted over recent decades [2].

## The Galilean moons

Galileo's 1610 observation of four moons orbiting Jupiter provided direct evidence that not all celestial bodies circle Earth, and was consequential for the acceptance of heliocentrism [2].

Io is the most volcanically active body known, heated by tidal flexing. Europa very likely holds a subsurface saltwater ocean beneath its ice shell, making it a priority target in the search for habitable environments. Ganymede is the largest moon in the Solar System and the only one with its own magnetic field.

adult.summary: A hydrogen-helium gas giant of 318 Earth masses whose interior structure, magnetosphere and satellite system make it a system in miniature.
adult.body:
Jupiter is the fifth planet from the Sun and the most massive body in the Solar System after the Sun, at approximately 1.898 x 10^27 kg — some 2.5 times the combined mass of the remaining planets [1].

## Interior

Bulk composition approximates solar abundances, dominated by hydrogen and helium with enrichment in heavier elements relative to the Sun. There is no solid surface; the atmosphere grades continuously into a supercritical fluid envelope, and beyond roughly a megabar hydrogen transitions to a metallic, electrically conducting state.

The Juno mission's gravity science substantially revised the interior picture. Rather than a compact heavy-element core, the data are best fit by a dilute or fuzzy core extending across a considerable fraction of the planetary radius, with heavy elements partially mixed into the envelope. This has implications for formation models, since core accretion had generally predicted a more concentrated core [2].

## Magnetosphere

Dynamo action in metallic hydrogen produces a surface field roughly an order of magnitude stronger than Earth's and a magnetosphere that, were it visible, would subtend several times the angular diameter of the Moon from Earth. Io's volcanism supplies a plasma torus that dominates magnetospheric dynamics, and the resulting radiation environment is severe enough to constrain spacecraft design.

## Atmospheric dynamics

The banded appearance reflects alternating zonal jets of remarkable stability. Juno's microwave radiometry demonstrated that these structures extend to depths of thousands of kilometres rather than being shallow weather-layer phenomena.

The Great Red Spot is a long-lived anticyclone. Continuous observational records extend to 1878; whether Cassini's seventeenth-century observations of a Permanent Spot describe the same vortex is unresolved and should not be asserted. Systematic shrinkage in its longitudinal extent is well documented over the twentieth and twenty-first centuries [2].

## Satellite system

At least 95 satellites are confirmed, with the total continuing to rise as survey sensitivity improves; any stated count should be treated as a lower bound at a given date rather than a fixed property [2].

The Galilean satellites are of first-order scientific importance. Io exhibits the highest volcanic heat flux of any known body, powered by tidal dissipation in the Laplace resonance. Europa's induced magnetic response provides strong evidence for a global subsurface saline ocean, and it is a principal target of astrobiological interest. Ganymede is the largest satellite in the Solar System and uniquely possesses an intrinsic magnetic field.

Galileo's 1610 detection of these four bodies is historically decisive: it demonstrated the existence of a centre of motion other than Earth, undermining a core objection to heliocentrism [2].
